title: Is this organization tailoring appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether a way of applying or tailoring the organization practice in a scenario is effective, and pick the reason that actually explains the verdict.
question: At Larkspur Rail, the project manager decides to prioritize user stories across all three delivery teams himself, to keep the app consistent. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?

teach.h: What 'effective organization' looks like in agile
teach.body: An organization item asks whether a structure, role arrangement, product or technique fits the project. Test it against the guidance (one PM, a PO per team, the CPO across teams, the agile coach at organization level), the products (commercial approach, team structure, role descriptions) and the techniques (skill matrix, delegation poker, delegation matrix). Good tailoring keeps clear accountability while giving teams room to self-manage.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pinewick click and collect
teach.body: IT operations manager Kieran Walsh wants every website change to go through a weekly change board. Agile coach Nikhil Rao works with the board and Kieran on this: appropriate, because the agile coach removes systemic blockers to agile adoption. Patrick Dunne, the PM, wants to rank stories across both teams himself: not appropriate, because the CPO sets priorities across teams. The store operations team builds its skill matrix at kickoff and shows it on its new team dashboard: appropriate.

head: Situation
Deciding rule

PO has direct authority over the team

teach.text: Many wrong options are true but beside the point, such as 'the PM runs the project day to day' offered to justify the PM prioritizing across teams. The PM does run the project, but cross-team priorities belong to the CPO.

Team coach asked to fix board resistance

items: One PM however many teams; a PO per team; the CPO prioritizes across teams.
PM has direct authority over the PO; the PO over team members.
Agile coach: organization-level, systemic blockers. Team coach: one or two teams.
Skill matrix and delegation are co-created with the team, then made visible.
Choose the reason that decides the case, not a nearby true statement.

summary: You can now judge whether an organization structure, role arrangement, product entry or technique is effective in an agile scenario. You can also name the rule that decides the verdict and reject reasons that are true but beside the point.

A.q: At Pinewick, the IT operations manager insists that every website change goes through a weekly change board, which blocks the e-commerce team's frequent releases. Agile coach Nikhil Rao works with the project board and the IT operations manager to address this. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the agile coach removes systemic blockers
Yes, because the agile coach owns the release schedule
No, because the team coach should deal with blockers
No, because project assurance monitors agile adherence
A.why: The agile coach works across teams to identify and remove systemic blockers to agile adoption, and supports the board and PM with agile expertise (Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: The release map is the project's plan; the agile coach does not own it.
whyNot.2: The team coach works inside one or two teams; an organization-level blocker is for the agile coach.
whyNot.3: Assurance does monitor adherence, but it does not work to remove adoption blockers.

A.q: Larkspur Rail has three delivery teams, each with a product owner. To keep the app consistent, the project manager decides to prioritize user stories across all three teams himself. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM manages the project day to day
Yes, because the PM has direct authority over the POs
No, because each PO should prioritize across all teams
No, because the CPO defines priorities across the teams
A.why: The chief product owner makes sure priorities are clearly defined across teams (Table 7.2). The PM is a servant leader linking governance and teams, not the cross-team prioritizer.

whyNot.0: True, but day-to-day management does not include setting priorities across teams.
whyNot.1: The PM does have direct authority over the POs, but that is not authority over cross-team priorities.
whyNot.2: A PO owns one team's backlog and does not prioritize across teams.

A.q: Saltmarsh's project manager completes the service design team's skill matrix herself from staff records and keeps it in her project files. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
options: Yes, because a skill matrix identifies training needs
Yes, because the PM assigns people to their tasks
No, because it is co-created and shown on the dashboard
No, because skills belong in the role descriptions
A.why: The team skill matrix is completed collaboratively in the project kickoff workshop and, for delivery teams, displayed on the team dashboard (7.4.1, Table 13.8).

whyNot.0: True, but it does not make a matrix written alone and hidden effective.
whyNot.1: The matrix does help put the right people on tasks, but it is built collaboratively with the team, not by the PM from records.
whyNot.3: Role descriptions hold role responsibilities, not individual skills and gaps.

B.q: At Callowmere, the project manager writes into the role descriptions that wellbeing staff will join sprint reviews online on Tuesdays and come to campus every other Thursday. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
options: Yes, because role descriptions set how people work together
Yes, because remote staff need their duties written down
No, because these arrangements go in the team structure
No, because they belong in the commercial approach
B.why: Arrangements for co-location or remote teams are working practices in the project management team structure; role descriptions hold each role's specific responsibilities (Table 7.3).

whyNot.0: How people work together is the team structure's job, not the role descriptions'.
whyNot.1: Duties do go in role descriptions, but these are working arrangements, not duties.
whyNot.3: The commercial approach covers procurement and contracts.

B.q: Easterholm's project manager proposes keeping the Abacus agreement as it is: every change to the interface needs a fixed-price change request that takes six weeks to quote. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
options: Yes, because cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan
Yes, because a fixed price protects the council's grant
No, because supplier terms belong in role descriptions
No, because the contract form should support agile work
B.why: The commercial management approach should make the procurement and contract form support agile development, for example fixed teams or costs per iteration and an agreed DoD (Table 7.3). Six-week quotes for every change work against iterative delivery.

whyNot.0: True, but a cost per iteration also keeps cost fixed; this does not justify slow change requests.
whyNot.1: Protecting the grant matters, but the guidance is about a contract form that supports agile.
whyNot.2: Contract terms are in the commercial management approach.

B.q: Draycott appoints Tomasz Zielinski, the software team's Scrum master, as team coach for the software team and also for the engineers' trial team. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
options: Yes, because a team coach works with one or two teams
Yes, because a team coach removes organization blockers
No, because every team needs its own separate team coach
No, because a Scrum master cannot hold a PRINCE2 Agile role
B.why: A team coach works closely with one or two specific teams (Table 7.2, 7.3.1), and a Scrum master fits the team coach role.

whyNot.1: Removing systemic, organization-level blockers is the agile coach's role.
whyNot.2: Team coaches may work with one or two teams.
whyNot.3: A Scrum master maps well to the team coach role.

C.q: To speed up decisions, Callowmere's project manager sets up the team structure so that the Northmere Systems developers report directly to him instead of through a product owner. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM runs the project on the board's behalf
Yes, because supplier teams report to the project manager
No, because the PO holds direct authority over team members
No, because the team coach directs supplier developers
C.why: The PM is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, and the PO is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members; work is agreed PM to PO as sets of user stories (7.3.1).

whyNot.0: True, but the PM exercises that authority through the PO, not over developers directly.
whyNot.1: Supplier and in-house teams alike work through a product owner.
whyNot.3: The team coach helps the team self-manage; it has no line authority.

C.q: In Pinewick's kickoff workshop, the e-commerce team and the store operations team each use delegation poker to agree their decision levels, then show them in a team delegation matrix on their dashboards. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because a delegation matrix replaces role descriptions
Yes, because agreed, visible delegation supports self-management
No, because the store team uses Kanban rather than Scrum
No, because the PM should set decision levels for teams
C.why: Delegation poker defines decision-making collaboratively (7.4.2), and the delegation matrix makes it transparent (7.4.3); the kickoff topic aims to simplify decisions and empower self-management (Table 13.8).

whyNot.0: Role descriptions remain a management product; the matrix complements them.
whyNot.2: The techniques suit any team, whatever its framework.
whyNot.3: Imposing decision levels works against the self-management these techniques support.

C.q: Draycott's commercial management approach for Senticore sets a fixed price, defines the minimum viable product as sensors on ten machines for Release 1, and sets a tolerance on the number of machines covered. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because a fixed price means the scope is fixed as well
Yes, because the contract can define the MVP and tolerances
No, because hardware contracts cannot include agile terms
No, because the MVP is identified in the project canvas
C.why: The commercial management approach should make the contract support agile, for example by defining the MVP and possible tolerances (Table 7.3).

whyNot.0: Scope flexes above the Must haves; here the tolerance on machines is exactly that flexibility.
whyNot.2: The guidance on contract form is not limited to software, and this contract does support agile delivery.
whyNot.3: The canvas does identify the MVP, but that does not stop the contract defining it too.

reteach.title: Ask: whose job is it really?
reteach.question: When an organization proposal feels wrong, how do you find the rule it breaks?

blocks.h: Map the job to the role
blocks.body: Most organization verdicts come down to one question: is the right role or product doing this job? Cross-team priorities belong to the CPO. Day-to-day direction of developers goes through the PO. Organization-wide resistance goes to the agile coach. Working arrangements go in the team structure, duties in role descriptions, contract form in the commercial approach. If the stem gives the job to someone else, the verdict is usually No.

blocks.text: Roles may be combined, so 'one person, two roles' is not automatically wrong. Check whether the duties fit.

explain.body: The PM agrees work with the PO as a set of user stories; the PO leads the team. Going around the PO breaks the structure.

test.q: Pinewick's project manager wants the store operations team to prepare three new stores next. Sophie Draper is the team's product owner. What should he do?
options: Agree the work with Sophie as user stories
Give the order to the team's coach to pass on
Ask the CPO to direct the team members
Post the new stores on the team's dashboard
test.why: The PM agrees work packages with the PO as sets of user stories; the PO has direct authority over the team (7.3.1).

whyNot.1: The team coach has no line authority and is not a channel for work packages.
whyNot.2: The CPO sets cross-team priorities but does not direct team members.
whyNot.3: The team dashboard is the team's own; work is agreed with the PO.

explain.body: The CPO owns the project backlog and defines priorities across teams. Each PO owns one team's product backlog, aligned with the project backlog. The PM does neither.

test.q: At Callowmere, the web team's PO and the Northmere team's PO disagree about which of their features should come first in Release 2. Who should resolve this?
options: The project manager
The chief product owner
The web team's coach
The project executive
test.why: The CPO makes sure priorities are clearly defined across teams (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The PM facilitates between governance and teams but does not set cross-team priorities.
whyNot.2: The team coach supports one or two teams; it does not set priorities.
whyNot.3: The executive is accountable and approves tolerances; priorities across teams are the CPO's.

explain.body: The agile coach helps the organization adopt and sustain agile, works across teams on systemic blockers and supports the board, assurance and PM. The team coach works inside one or two teams.
explain.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1

test.q: Easterholm's assistant director wants written monthly reports and does not want to be bothered with dashboards, which is slowing agile adoption. Which role should help address this resistance?
options: Agile coach
Team coach
Project support
Project assurance
test.why: The agile coach works across teams to remove systemic blockers to agile adoption and supports leaders with agile expertise (Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: The team coach works within one or two teams, not with senior leaders.
whyNot.2: Project support could produce reports, but that would not address the resistance.
whyNot.3: Assurance monitors adherence; it does not coach leaders through adoption.

explain.body: Working practices and arrangements (remote tools, co-location, reviews, access) belong in the project management team structure. Specific duties go in role descriptions. Contract form goes in the commercial approach.

test.q: Larkspur records the remote-working tools that the Coinbridge team will share with the in-house teams in the project management team structure. Which reason BEST supports this?
options: It holds each role's specific duties
It defines the supplier's contract terms
It records skills gaps for each team
It holds working practices and arrangements
test.why: The team structure includes working practices and arrangements, including co-location or remote arrangements and tools for transparency and rich communication (Table 7.3).

whyNot.0: Specific duties are in role descriptions.
whyNot.1: Contract terms are in the commercial management approach.
whyNot.2: Skills gaps are in the team skill matrix.
